letter.title: Open Letter to the Candidates for Minnesota Attorney General
letter.markdown:
**JOSEPH KIRCHNER**  
4440 Parklawn Avenue, #203  
Edina, MN 55435  
joseph@kirchner.ink  
(612) 552-2122

**OPEN LETTER TO THE CANDIDATES FOR MINNESOTA ATTORNEY GENERAL**

October 10, 2026

BY CERTIFIED MAIL, BY EMAIL, AND PUBLIC RELEASE

Keith Ellison, Candidate for Attorney General  
Keith Ellison for Attorney General committee  
PO Box 17224  
Minneapolis, MN 55417  
campaign@keithellison.org

Ron Schutz, Candidate for Attorney General  
Ron for MN AG  
216 Myrtle St W  
P.O. Box 132  
Stillwater, MN 55082-4830  
info@RonForMNAG.com

**Re:** Minnesota Statutes § 8.31, Subdivision 1: the office's public position, its position in federal court, and three questions for each candidate

Dear Mr. Ellison and Mr. Schutz:

I write as a Minnesota citizen to both of you, on the same day and in the same words, with three questions about the office you are asking to hold. This letter is public. On the day it is mailed to you it goes to the Minnesota reporters covering the office and the fraud cases, with its enclosure. Your answers, or the absence of them, will be sent to the same reporters and published on October 21, 2026.

**What I asked the office.** On February 10, 2026, I hand-delivered to the Office of the Attorney General a referral documenting consumer fraud and computer crimes by four companies operating in Minnesota across county lines, supported by exhibits. It invoked the Prevention of Consumer Fraud Act, Minn. Stat. §§ 325F.68–.70, and asked the office to investigate, to issue civil investigative demands, and to pursue civil enforcement, among other things.

**What the office answered.** On February 26, 2026, the office wrote: "the Minnesota Legislature delegated the authority to prosecute criminal matters to the county attorney. It did not delegate any such authority to this Office, nor did it delegate the authority to investigate criminal matters to this Office." The office's website says the same: the Legislature "delegated the authority to prosecute criminal matters to the county attorney. It did not delegate such authority to this Office." The letter did not mention § 8.31. It did not answer the civil requests. I am the plaintiff in *Kirchner v. Ellison*, No. 26-cv-2594 (D. Minn.), now on appeal, which arises from that letter.

**What the statute says.** Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 1: "The attorney general shall investigate violations of the law of this state respecting unfair, discriminatory, and other unlawful practices in business, commerce, or trade, and specifically, but not exclusively, … the Prevention of Consumer Fraud Act (sections 325F.68 to 325F.70) …". Minn. Stat. § 645.44, subd. 16: "'Shall' is mandatory."

**What the office says in court.** The office has defended the February 26 statement as accurate about criminal matters, telling the court the letter "contains no misstatement of law" (Doc. 16 at 5) and that the Attorney General "may only exercise the prosecutorial powers of a county attorney at the direction of the governor or via consent from a county attorney" (Doc. 11 at 8). At the same time it conceded that the office "must investigate" violations of the Consumer Fraud Act (Doc. 16 at 5), and argued in the alternative that even if the letter and the website "do misstate the law," I have no redress because investigation is discretionary (Doc. 16 at 6). The court dismissed on that alternative, "even if Kirchner is correct" that the office has the authority (Doc. 27 at 5). Nothing in my suit asks the office to give up its discretion over what it investigates or prosecutes. The suit asks whether the office has the authority the statutes name, and whether it will say so. The record is set out in the enclosure, point 7.

**What each of you said on October 2, 2026** (MPR News, Politics Friday; times are from the recording published on YouTube). On the civil duty, Mr. Ellison, at 2:49: "Minnesota Statute 8.31 requires, it says shall, the attorney general shall investigate all illegality, unfairness and discrimination in the area of business, commerce and trade. And I have lived up to that as early as this morning." On criminal matters, Mr. Ellison, at 12:37: "They're investigators … They are career prosecutors and the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension. We just brought a bunch of cases this week"; at 21:19: "I also am assisting local prosecutors in the investigation and in one case, prosecution of the people who were shot by ICE agents"; at 44:06: "We just convicted somebody in Winona who was a coach and criminally victimized three people." Mr. Schutz, at 4:34: "The attorney general is tasked under Minnesota statutes with original criminal jurisdiction over Medicaid and medical assistance fraud"; at 10:31: "You prosecute people by charging them with at least three felony counts of fraud over $35,000"; and at 22:07–23:26, on the ICE shootings: "there needed to be a joint federal and state investigation … if it leads to prosecutions and the evidence warrants it, that's what should happen … I am more than happy to lead the charge." On the standard for acting against a company, Mr. Schutz, at 16:14: "if they committed wrongdoing and Minnesotans were harmed, the attorney general should take action against that"; asked whether that is the standard he uses, Mr. Ellison, at 16:24: "Well, obviously, but that's just the basics."

**The three questions.** Each can be answered yes or no.

1. Will the office, under you, recognize its authority under Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 1 to investigate a citizen's referral of unlawful business practices, including consumer fraud, on its own, without a request from a county attorney or the Governor, the duty Mr. Ellison stated on October 2?

2. Will the office, under you, recognize that its authority to investigate criminal matters, and to cause and conduct their prosecution, is not limited to Medicaid fraud: that it rests on Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 2, on the office's own information, and on § 8.01, with the request pathways that section names, and that the Legislature recognized it again in 2025 in § 299C.061, subd. 4(c); and will the office withdraw the statement, in the letter and on the website, that the Legislature did not delegate such authority to this Office?

3. Will the office, under you, answer a citizen's referral with a decision on its merits, exercising whatever discretion the law gives, rather than with a statement that it lacks the authority?

I submit these questions as a lifelong Minnesota resident who places great weight on the Office of the Attorney General, and not in my capacity as a party to a lawsuit. Your answers cannot confer standing in my case or stand in for the Eighth Circuit's ruling; that belongs to the court, on the record. Every public office, and everyone elected to it, is bounded by its authority. Voters can cast an informed vote for the office only when a candidate's understanding of that authority matches the office's. Here, what each of you said on October 2 contradicts, or is hard to square with, what the office says in federal court. For the sake of Minnesota voters, I ask you to say which it is.

I ask for your written answers by October 21, 2026. On October 21, 2026 I will send the same reporters what each of you answered, or that you did not, so that voters may read it before Election Day. Answers may be sent to the email address above or by mail. The enclosure sets out each quotation above with its source. The full transcript and the record citations are available at kirchner.ink/mn-ag-candidates-open-letter.

Respectfully,

JOSEPH KIRCHNER

enclosure.markdown:
# ENCLOSURE A: The record and the debate, point by point

**To the open letter of October 10, 2026 to the candidates for Minnesota Attorney General.** Seven points, each with the office's words in the record and the candidates' words in public; every quotation is given with its source. Debate times are from the recording of the MPR News Politics Friday debate of October 2, 2026 as published on YouTube ("Minnesota Attorney General Debate: Keith Ellison vs. Ron Schutz | Full Debate"). Record citations are to *Kirchner v. Ellison*, No. 26-cv-2594 (D. Minn.): "Ex. A" is Exhibit A to the Complaint (ECF 1-2); "Doc. 37" is the Attorney General's memorandum of October 7, 2026 (ECF 37).

**1. The statute's duty.**

*In the record.* The February 26 letter (Ex. A at 2) does not mention § 8.31. In court the office defends the letter as discretion, Doc. 37 at 5: "the AGO could still reject the petition for any reason at all without it constituting an injury to Plaintiff."

*In public.* Mr. Ellison, 2:49: "Minnesota Statute 8.31 requires, it says shall, the attorney general shall investigate all illegality, unfairness and discrimination in the area of business, commerce and trade. And I have lived up to that as early as this morning."

**2. Investigation.**

*In the record.* Ex. A at 2: "nor did it delegate the authority to investigate criminal matters to this Office."

*In public.* Mr. Ellison, 12:37–12:52: "They're investigators … They are career prosecutors and the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension. We just brought a bunch of cases this week." 21:19: "I also am assisting local prosecutors in the investigation and in one case, prosecution of the people who were shot by ICE agents." 25:24: "Yes, we're going to investigate." Mr. Schutz, 22:07–23:26: "there needed to be a joint federal and state investigation … if it leads to prosecutions and the evidence warrants it, that's what should happen … I am more than happy to lead the charge."

**3. Referral to the FBI.**

*In the record.* Ex. A at 2–3: the office directed the citizen to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center: "You may contact the IC3 and make a request to investigate."

*In public.* Mr. Ellison, 8:51–9:00, on Feeding Our Future: "we began to work with the FBI. And later there were search warrants executed. There was then indictments."

**4. Prosecution.**

*In the record.* Ex. A at 2: "the Minnesota Legislature delegated the authority to prosecute criminal matters to the county attorney. It did not delegate any such authority to this Office." The office's website (Compl. ¶ 22; Ex. B at 4): "It delegated the authority to prosecute criminal matters to the county attorney. It did not delegate such authority to this Office."

*In public.* Mr. Ellison, 5:57: "We bring the charges. We get the convictions." 44:06: "We just convicted somebody in Winona who was a coach and criminally victimized three people." 57:33: "I've convicted over 350 people of Medicaid fraud, one every eight days." Mr. Schutz, 4:34: "The attorney general is tasked under Minnesota statutes with original criminal jurisdiction over Medicaid and medical assistance fraud." 10:31: "You prosecute people by charging them with at least three felony counts of fraud over $35,000."

**5. The standard for acting.**

*In the record.* The office's position in court is that a citizen "does not have a constitutional right to have his referral investigated" (ECF 11 at 13) and that a referral may be refused "for any reason at all" (Doc. 37 at 5).

*In public.* Mr. Schutz, 16:14: "if they committed wrongdoing and Minnesotans were harmed, the attorney general should take action against that." Mr. Ellison, 16:24, asked whether that is his standard: "Well, obviously, but that's just the basics." Mr. Schutz, 54:48: "If they're not complying with some law, then it's the job of the Attorney General to step in."

**6. Discretion.**

*In the record.* Doc. 37 at 5 treats the February 26 statement that the office lacks authority as an exercise of discretion.

*In public.* Mr. Schutz, 11:22–11:55: "the attorney general has broad discretion. As to how he allocates resources within the office … I have the discretion within the office as to where to devote resources."

**7. The office in court.**

*In the record.* The office has defended the February 26 statement as accurate: the letter "does not disavow the AGO's jurisdiction to investigate violations of PCFA, only the ability to investigate and prosecute criminal matters," so "there is no 'misstatement of law'" (Doc. 11 at 8); "The February 26 letter contains no misstatement of law" (Doc. 16 at 5); the Attorney General "may only exercise the prosecutorial powers of a county attorney at the direction of the governor or via consent from a county attorney" (Doc. 11 at 8). At the same time it told the court that "neither party disputes" the office's authority to investigate violations of the Consumer Fraud Act and that the office "must investigate" them, while denying that the statutes give it "broad criminal authority" (Doc. 16 at 4–5); and, in the alternative, it argued that "assuming … the Attorney General's website and the February 26 letter do misstate the law," the citizen has no redress because investigation is discretionary and no standing to complain (Doc. 16 at 6; Doc. 11 at 9, 13). The court dismissed on that ground, "even if Kirchner is correct" that the office has the authority (Doc. 27 at 5), and the office's latest filing says it "could still reject the petition for any reason at all" (Doc. 37 at 5). The letter has not been withdrawn, and the website said the same when last captured on March 18, 2026.

*In public.* Mr. Ellison, 2:49, 12:37, 21:19 and 44:06; Mr. Schutz, 4:34, 10:31 and 22:07–23:26, as set out at points 1, 2 and 4 above.

**The statute.** Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 1 (2025): "The attorney general shall investigate violations of the law of this state respecting unfair, discriminatory, and other unlawful practices in business, commerce, or trade, and specifically, but not exclusively, the Nonprofit Corporation Act (sections 317A.001 to 317A.909), the Act Against Unfair Discrimination and Competition (sections 325D.01 to 325D.07), the Unlawful Trade Practices Act (sections 325D.09 to 325D.16), the Antitrust Act (sections 325D.49 to 325D.66), section 325F.67 and other laws against false or fraudulent advertising, the antidiscrimination acts contained in section 325D.67, the act against monopolization of food products (section 325D.68), the act regulating telephone advertising services (section 325E.39), the Prevention of Consumer Fraud Act (sections 325F.68 to 325F.70), and chapter 53A regulating currency exchanges and assist in the enforcement of those laws as in this section provided." Minn. Stat. § 645.44, subd. 16: "'Shall' is mandatory."

**The statutes behind question 2** (as filed with the Complaint, Exhibit E, ECF 3-1). Minn. Stat. § 8.31, subd. 2: "When the attorney general has information providing a reasonable ground to believe that any person has violated, or is about to violate, any of the laws of this state referred to in subdivision 1, the attorney general shall have power to investigate those violations, or suspected violations, and to take such steps as are necessary to cause the arrest and prosecution of all persons violating any of the statutes specifically mentioned in subdivision 1 or any other laws respecting unfair, discriminatory, or other unlawful practices in business, commerce, or trade." Minn. Stat. § 8.01: "Upon request of the county attorney, the attorney general shall appear in court in such criminal cases as the attorney general deems proper. … Whenever the governor shall so request, in writing, the attorney general shall prosecute any person charged with an indictable offense, and in all such cases may attend upon the grand jury and exercise the powers of a county attorney." Minn. Stat. § 299C.061 (Financial Crimes and Fraud Section, as amended in 2025), subd. 4(c): "Notwithstanding paragraph (b), this section has no effect on the authority of the attorney general to investigate and enforce violations or suspected violations of Minnesota civil or criminal law."

**The referral's requests** (Ex. A, referral § V): (1) open a criminal investigation; (2) issue civil investigative demands; (3) coordinate with federal authorities; (4) pursue criminal prosecution where the evidence supports charges; (5) pursue civil enforcement under Minnesota consumer protection statutes; (6) preserve evidence. The February 26 letter addressed items 1 and 4 by disclaimer, answered item 3 only by directing the citizen to the FBI's web portal, and did not address items 2, 5 or 6.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'm not sure if you can hear me. Good afternoon. This is MPR News. I'm Brian Bakst. We have a special Politics Friday today. And just over a month, Minnesota voters will decide who should lead the state's main public law office. The Attorney General carries significant power to drive litigation, defend state interest, aid in criminal prosecution, and work with legislators to shape new laws. The Attorney General sits on a state board that manages tens of billions of dollars in investments. And holdings for pensions and similar accounts. The Attorney General is one of three people who weigh pardon applications. And the Attorney General has a say in the durability of executive orders issued by the governor. With us for the next hour are two people seeking that title for the next four years. Keith Ellison is a DFLer who's held the Attorney General role for the two terms beginning in 2019. Good afternoon.

turns.speaker: KE
turns.text: Thank you, Brian. Thanks for having me.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And Ron Schutz is a civil litigator who has most recently led a major Twin Cities law firm. Happy to have you here as well.

turns.speaker: RS
turns.text: Thank you, Brian. Thanks for having me.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: So there aren't a lot of ground rules to go over, gentlemen. There are no timed responses, but we're asking you to be as succinct as possible in your answers so we can get to as many topics as possible. We'll allow for rebuttal, we're warranted, but please do your best to avoid talking over one another. And for the radio audience, you can find a live video feed of this debate at MPRnews.org or come back later if you missed something.

turns.speaker: KE/RS
turns.text: We all set? I'm all set.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: So, Keith Ellison, when you were inaugurated for the first time, you vowed to be the people's lawyer whose job is, quote, to help Minnesotans afford their lives. With dignity and respect, how have you measured up?

turns.speaker: KE
turns.text: I think we have succeeded. I can tell you, Brian, when you mentioned take me back eight years, I think of Nicole Holtz-Smith, who was a woman who approached me when I was a member of Congress and told me about her son who went from her insurance to his own. He went from paying nothing for insulin to paying about $1,300 a month. He tried to ration his insulin but was unable to do that. His body went into ketoacidosis and he died. When I became attorney general, one of the first cases that I filed was against the insulin cartel. And now, in Minnesota, insulin is kept at $35. This has been the operating principle of my service, helping people afford their lives and live with dignity, safety, and respect. Minnesota Statute 8.31 requires, it says shall, the attorney general shall investigate all illegality, unfairness and discrimination in the area of business, commerce and trade. And I have lived up to that as early as this morning.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And Ron Schutz, this is your first one for a public elected office. Prior to launching your campaign, you were on a finalist list to be Minnesota's U.S. Attorney. But why this job and why now?

turns.speaker: RS
turns.text: Well, Brian, you're correct. I was on the finalist list to be United States Attorney. And when that didn't happen, when Dan Rosen was selected as U.S. Attorney, my phone started ringing off the hook because I had previously, considered running for public office, been urged to run for public office several times in the past. And for various reasons, timing, commitments with my law firm and others, I decided not to do that. But I stepped down from being chairman of my law firm in 2024. And I was looking for what I was going to do next in life. I've started my career in public service by being an officer in the United States Army. And I don't like the direction the state is headed. And I'm sure I'll do that. I'll get to address several of those issues during the course of this debate. I've got three grandchildren that live in this state. And I prefer that they grow up in a state that looks a lot more like the one I grew up in and was known as the land of 10,000 lakes and not the state as it's currently known as the land of 10,000 frauds.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Well, without question, investigations and prosecutions of fraud have stoked public frustration over misuse of tax dollars. Ron Schutz, what do you see as the role of the attorney general in combating that?

turns.speaker: RS
turns.text: Well, the role of the attorney general is very broad in combating that fraud. The attorney general is tasked under Minnesota statutes with original criminal jurisdiction over Medicaid and medical assistance fraud. And in my view, I don't think this attorney general has done a good job prosecuting those cases, claims to have prosecuted 350 cases. KSTP, a local news station in town, did an investigative report. They looked at 250 cases. They looked at 250 cases that Keith Ellison had prosecuted and found the overwhelming, in the overwhelming majority of those cases, nobody went to jail, nobody had a felony on their record, and if anything, they paid cents on the dollars. And that is because the way the cases were prosecuted. In 70 of those cases, they found that there were stays of adjudication where the person was put on parole, came out of parole. And then the charges were dropped. So no convictions, at least 70 of those cases.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Well, Keith Ellison, he's assessed your role as not having done as much as you've said. What do you want to say about that?

turns.speaker: KE
turns.text: I say he's absolutely wrong. I'm very proud of the 350 convictions that my office has secured. I'm proud of the group that does that work every single day. Mr. Schutz doesn't seem to understand that it is courts who sentence defendants, not the prosecutors. We bring the charges. We get the convictions. The courts sentence people. And so he's confusing those two roles. But here's the thing. I also worked with the legislature to negotiate a bill that lengthened sentences. He's concerned about sentences. We've actually got a bill that lengthened sentences, brought back longer period of time to get restitution orders, and was able to secure 18 more new people from my office with a three to one to three match from the federal government to us. We put up one buck. They put up three. Now, we've passed that law into law, but Mr. Schutz opposed this piece of legislation. He wrote a press release trying to get people to kill the bill. So it seems to me that he might be against Ellison, but he's not against fraud, because if he was against fraud, he would not care who was pushing that bill. He would have stood with me and helped get more strength for our office.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Did you oppose the bill that Keith Ellison was talking about?

turns.speaker: RS
turns.text: Well, first. We need to clarify one thing. Under Minnesota Statute 609.095, the prosecution can agree with the defense to have the judge enter a stay of adjudication. That was done in at least 70 of those cases. So I'm absolutely right about that. You can check the record. And what happens is no conviction is entered on the record. And in 144 cases, there was a stay of imposition of sentence. What that means is there's a plea offered. The judge accepts the plea. Puts the person on probation. If the person successfully completes probation, then the felony to which they have pled is reduced to a misdemeanor.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: But briefly, did you oppose the legislation?

turns.speaker: RS
turns.text: Well, that's incomplete with what I said. My statement was this attorney general has substantial resources in the office not being deployed toward combating fraud. And he needs his priorities are wrong. He needs to reprioritize combating fraud.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Keith Ellison, particularly when it comes to the most...

turns.speaker: KE
turns.text: He didn't answer the question about whether he opposed the bill or not.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Particularly when it comes to the most visible case, Feeding Our Future. Right. When did your office first step in and how?

turns.speaker: KE
turns.text: Well, we represented the Department of Education. And when Feeding Our Future was asking, was demanding more money than they were entitled to, the Department of Education said, no, we weren't going to give, they weren't going to give that money over because there was no proof for it. We didn't know how deep the problem was. But we knew that there was a problem because the billings and the invoices didn't match. I defended the Department of Education, even when Feeding Our Future sued them and scurrilously claimed to be victims of discrimination. We fought that right up until Feeding Our Future. These people lied to judges. They lied to journalists. And they tried to lie their way through court. Then what we did is we began to work with the FBI. And later there were search warrants executed. There was then indictments. And now those people are in prison as they should be. My office worked very hard to make sure that justice was done. When we couldn't get it through the court system we thought we should get it through, we worked with our federal allies and got them convicted there.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Well, staying with you for a minute, you've been questioned before Congress and other venues for meeting with and paying contributions for people who were later accused in that nutrition aid scheme. What happened there?

turns.speaker: KE
turns.text: I'm glad you asked me about that, Brian, because here's the thing. Nobody who I see, I meet with people every single day. I had several meetings this week, and so I met -- these people wanted to meet with me, and I met with them because I meet with people. But I took nothing from them. I did nothing for them. And no one in that meeting gave me a campaign donation. In fact, one of them suggested campaign donations. I said, no, this is an official meeting. That's on the tape you're talking about. But then what happened is that when those people sent me some campaign donations, no one in the meeting, others, I sent them back. Brian, to the federal authorities. So I have received no campaign donations from these people, and we aided in the prosecution and conviction of these people. I'm glad they're in prison, and I'm proud of the work that my team did to do that.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ron Schutz, going forward, the attorney general's office will have a more robust Medicaid fraud control unit with additional staff, expanded powers to investigate. How do you foresee using that?

turns.speaker: RS
turns.text: Well, I want to go back to how these cases are handled. People need to go to jail. Nobody's afraid out there. There are no repercussions. And here's how people go to jail. You prosecute people by charging them with at least three felony counts of fraud over $35,000. And then you refuse to enter into sweetheart plea agreements because if you then try these cases, and you've got to remember, I approach this job and will approach this job as a trial lawyer and not as a politician. So I view the way to do these cases is to actually go to court, stand up before juries and judges, get prosecuted. If you get a conviction on three felony counts for theft above $35,000, which is relatively easy to do given the scope of the fraud here, there's mandatory prison sentence under the state sentencing guidelines if you look at the grid.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: What about the Medicaid fraud control unit? Do you think the amount of staff, 18 new staff members, is enough?

turns.speaker: RS
turns.text: No. I would devote additional resources to that, and I'm glad you asked that question, Brian, because the attorney general has broad discretion. As to how he allocates resources within the office. Each year, the attorney general files a report with the legislature about the activities in the office. The most recent report that was filed was 51 pages long. 51 pages. Only two pages of that report were devoted to fraud. I will devote additional resources to fighting fraud. I have the discretion within the office as to where to devote resources. I'll devote more resources to fighting fraud.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Keith Ellison, more than the 18.

turns.speaker: KE
turns.text: Well, I tell you. There are about 50 Medicaid control fraud units throughout the United States. They are evaluated from Washington because Washington gives about three bucks for every one dollar that the state puts up. And they have evaluated us as having an excellent program. They have said, look, you are punching way above your weight. Your people are getting convictions, and they support and have given us positive feedback on our program. And so I don't know what Ron is talking about. We do this work every day. And I can tell you, the people who do this work have no connection to politics at all. They are line prosecutors. They do prosecution every day. They're investigators, and I'm proud of the work that they do. And quite frankly, Mr. Schutz, I find it offensive for you to insult these people. They are career prosecutors and the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension. We just brought a bunch of cases this week. These people work hard to build these cases. We're getting these convictions. And, Mr. Schutz, why? Why did you oppose my bill? Why did you put a partisan consideration in front of trying to get more resources to prosecute fraud?

turns.speaker: RS
turns.text: Nobody goes to jail.

turns.speaker: KE
turns.text: Let me repeat that. You can people go to jail all the time. Go to listen.

turns.speaker: RS
turns.text: That's not true. Look at the KSTP report. Keith Ellison is on camera being confronted by the reporters. Nobody goes to report, goes to jail, and nobody ends up with a felony on your record. So the report that's submitted to the federal government about what the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit does measure certain factors. It does not measure whether people go to jail because if it measured that, it would get an F grade.

turns.speaker: MOD
